target_audience: University students or advanced high school students familiar with basic calculus

outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students familiar with basic calculus

sections.title: The Shift: From Slope to Stretching
sections.content: Introduce the shift in perspective from the static 'slope of a tangent line' on a graph to the dynamic 'local scaling factor' between two number lines. Explain that a function is a transformation that maps points from an input space to an output space.
sections.example: Imagine a rubber band representing the input number line. The function 'pulls' or 'compresses' parts of this rubber band to create the output line.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Functions as Mappings
sections.content: Visualize two parallel number lines: the Input (x) and the Output (f(x)). Show how a single point on the x-line maps to a point on the f(x)-line via colored arrows. This sets the stage for seeing derivatives as a ratio of lengths rather than coordinates.
sections.example: If an ant moves 1 unit on the Input line, we observe how far its 'shadow' moves on the Output line.

sections.title: Defining the Local Scaling Factor
sections.content: Focus on a tiny interval 'dx' around a point. The derivative f'(x) is the factor by which that tiny interval is stretched or shrunk when it moves to the output line (df). Formula: df ≈ f'(x) * dx. If f'(x) > 1, it's a stretch; if 0 < f'(x) < 1, it's a compression.
sections.example: At a specific point, if f'(x) = 3, a tiny step of 0.01 on the input line results in a 0.03 step on the output line—like a 3x magnifying glass.

sections.title: Visualizing Non-Linear Transformation (f(x) = x²)
sections.content: Apply the transformation view to f(x) = x². Show that at x=1, the scaling is 2 (moderate stretch), but at x=3, the scaling is 6 (intense stretch). This demonstrates that the 'stretching power' of the function changes depending on where you are.
sections.example: An animated 'heat map' on the input line where areas near higher x-values appear more stretched out as they map to the output line.

sections.title: Conclusion: Sensitivity and Density
sections.content: Summarize the derivative as a 'measure of sensitivity.' A high derivative means the output is highly sensitive to input changes. Connect this to density: where the derivative is high, the points are 'spread out' in the transformation; where it's low, they are 'packed together.'
sections.example: Think of a digital image filter: the derivative represents how much the filter distorts or 'zooms' into specific features of the original image.

storyboard.title: The Shift: From Slope to Stretching
lecture_lines: Traditionally, we see derivatives as slopes on graphs.
Let's view them as dynamic transformations instead.
Functions map an input space to an output space.
animations: Display title "The Shift: From Slope to Stretching" in #FFFFFF.
Show two horizontal lines, "Input" (#00FF00) and "Output" (#00BFFF), vertically separated.
A rubber band segment on the Input line morphs to a stretched version on the Output line.
Highlight a small segment on both lines, showing the scale difference labeled "Scaling Factor".

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Functions as Mappings
lecture_lines: Imagine two parallel lines for input and output.
Arrows show how input points map to output points.
This shifts focus from coordinates to relative lengths.
animations: Create two parallel lines, Input (#00FF00) and Output (#00BFFF).
Draw arrows pointing from specific values on Input to their results on Output.
A dot (#FFFF00) moves from 1 to 2 on the Input line.
A corresponding dot on the Output line moves a distance relative to the derivative.
Display text "Ratio = Output Move / Input Move" in #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: Defining the Local Scaling Factor
lecture_lines: Focus on a tiny interval, dx, around a point.
The function maps dx to output interval df.
The derivative is the local scaling factor.
Here, df equals the derivative times dx.
Scaling factor determines if intervals stretch or shrink.
animations: On Input line (#00FF00), highlight a small segment "dx" in #FFFF00.
Show mapped segment "df" on Output line (#00BFFF) in #FF0000.
Display formula "df \approx f'(x) \cdot dx" in #FFFFFF.
Show df being exactly 3 times the length of dx for f'(x) = 3.
Shrink df to half of dx, displaying f'(x) = 0.5.

storyboard.title: Visualizing Non-Linear Transformation (f(x) = x²)
lecture_lines: Observe the transformation for the function x squared.
At x equals one, the scaling factor is two.
At x equals three, the scaling increases to six.
The stretching power changes across the input line.
Larger inputs result in much more intense stretching.
animations: Show equation "f(x) = x^2" in #FFFFFF.
Highlight x=1 on Input; show mapped step on Output twice as large.
Shift focus to x=3 on Input line.
Show mapped step on Output becoming 6 times larger than Input.
Apply #FF4500 (orange-red) gradient to Input line to show "stretching power".

storyboard.title: Conclusion: Sensitivity and Density
lecture_lines: Derivatives measure output sensitivity to input changes.
High derivatives spread points out in the output.
Low derivatives pack points closer together.
animations: Show word "Sensitivity" in #FFFF00 at the center.
On Output line (#00BFFF), move a group of points further apart.
On Output line, move a group of points closer together.
A magnifying glass icon moves along Input line, showing zoomed Output results.
